english_translation: I am looking for my keys, but I do not see them on the table.

dialogue.shona: Ndiri kutsvaga makiyi angu asi handisi kuawona patafura.
dialogue.english: I am looking for my keys, but I do not see them on the table.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Ndiri [ndiri] • kutsvaga [to / at tsvaga] • makiyi [plural kiyi] • angu [angu] • asi [but / however] • handisi [I do not si] • kuawona [to / at awona] • patafura [on the table]

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('patafura')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'patafura'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('angu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'angu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

cultural_notes.title: Household Keys ('Makiyi') & Leaving Items on the Hall Table
cultural_notes.content: Before heading out to work or the market, families keep house and gate keys ('makiyi') in a central spot on the dining or living room table ('patafura') so everyone knows where to find them.

active_exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'mumba' and 'panze'?
options: 'mumba' means at school, while 'panze' means at work
'mumba' means inside the house, while 'panze' means outside
'mumba' means on the roof, while 'panze' means in the kitchen
'mumba' means rural village, while 'panze' means city centre
active_exercises.correct_answer: 'mumba' means inside the house, while 'panze' means outside
active_exercises.explanation: 'Mu-' denotes 'inside' ('mumba' = inside the house), whereas 'panze' means 'outside in the yard'.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Baba vari mumba asi vana vari kutamba panze.'
options: Mother went to the market to buy fruit and vegetables.
The books and keys are lying on the table.
Father is in the house, but the children are playing outside.
We are going to the rural home tomorrow morning.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Father is in the house, but the children are playing outside.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Baba vari mumba' = 'Father is in the house', 'asi' = 'but', 'vana vari kutamba panze' = 'the children are playing outside'.
